title: The Main Types of AI Models
subtitle: Match the task, input, and output

scenes.title: Start with the output
scenes.body: The deliverable tells you what capability to look for.
scenes.narration: An order issue arrives and the team needs three things. Someone must explain the validator, find the rule in our notes, and label the issue. Those tasks can share the same text, yet the outputs are different. Start by naming the deliverable. Once you know what must come back, you can pick a capability and a way to check the result.
scenes.code:
Explain code      → text
Find similar notes → ranked matches
Label a ticket    → category
Create an image   → pixels
Transcribe audio  → text
scenes.result: Start with the work the model must perform.
scenes.focus: Each task names a different deliverable
scenes.action: Match a training task to its desired output.

scenes.title: Explain and draft code
scenes.body: A language model can generate explanations or candidate changes.
scenes.narration: Give Copilot the return line and ask it to explain the result for zero and one. A language model can produce an explanation in ordinary words. Check those words against the expression. Both numbers satisfy this condition. If the answer says zero is rejected, you've found a specific sentence to question and a one-line source to point to.
scenes.code:
Explain this comparison for 0 and 1:
return quantity >= 0
scenes.result:
0 passes the current comparison.
1 also passes.
scenes.focus: The generated explanation can be checked against the expression
scenes.action: Ask Copilot to explain the two comparison results.

scenes.title: Find related notes
scenes.body: Embeddings represent inputs as vectors for similarity lookup.
scenes.narration: Now imagine the rule lives in one of three training notes. An embedding model turns the query and the stored notes into vectors. The system compares those representations and ranks possible matches. A useful first result is the order acceptance note. Open it and read the rule. Similarity helps you find a source. The source itself tells you what the rule says.
scenes.code:
Query: zero item order
Notes: order rules, release dates, colors
Embed query + compare stored note vectors
scenes.result:
Top match: order acceptance rules.
Open the original note for evidence.
scenes.focus: The order acceptance note ranks first in the example
scenes.action: Open the first result and read the cited rule.

scenes.title: Choose an allowed label
scenes.body: A classification task has a defined set of outcomes.
scenes.narration: For the issue label, our outputs are defect, feature, or question. The ticket reports behavior that already contradicts a documented rule. That gives us a reason to choose defect. A classifier can propose the label directly, and a language model can also choose from a short allowed list. Check which wording in the issue supports the decision before applying it.
scenes.code:
Allowed: defect | feature | question
Ticket: zero items accepted against the rule.
Return one label.
scenes.result:
defect
Check the proposed label before applying it.
scenes.focus: The example ticket receives the defect label
scenes.action: Choose one label and compare it to the documented rule.

scenes.title: Follow the input and output
scenes.body: Image understanding, image creation, and transcription differ.
scenes.narration: Think of the materials for a training lesson. A screenshot can go into a vision-capable model for a description. A written brief can go into an image model for an illustration. Audio can go into a transcription system for text. Check a screenshot description against the visible controls. Check a transcript against an important sentence in the recording.
scenes.code:
Screenshot → description
Text brief → training illustration
Audio clip → transcript
scenes.result: Pick capabilities based on the required output.
scenes.focus: Screenshot, picture and transcript have different outputs
scenes.action: Choose an input-output pair and name its check.

scenes.title: See the parts of a search
scenes.body: A system can combine several model types to answer one question.
scenes.narration: Some tools combine these steps. A question about zero quantities might first retrieve the most relevant note. The language model then uses that note to draft an answer. When you see the final paragraph, trace it back through the citation. If retrieval found an outdated rule, the answer can sound convincing and still use the wrong evidence.
scenes.code:
Question → embedding → related note
Related note + question → language model
Answer → read the cited source
scenes.result: Ask which step produced each piece of evidence.
scenes.focus: Retrieval supplies the note that generation can explain
scenes.action: Follow the query from retrieval to the cited note.

scenes.title: Choose and verify
scenes.body: Start with a task and define evidence of success.
scenes.narration: Choose a task from the training repository and finish this sentence. “I need this input turned into this output, and I will check it by doing this.” For example, use a language model to explain the validator and verify the explanation against the code and a test. Once that check is clear, you're ready to compare options.
scenes.code:
Explain validator → compare with tests.
Find related note → read the note.
Label an issue → compare to examples.
scenes.result: A capability choice plus a verification method.
scenes.focus: The chosen capability has a matching verification step
scenes.action: Write a task, its output, and one check.
